name: Itzhak Perlman
tagline: The violinist who refused to let polio silence his music
story:
In 1945, a four-year-old boy in Tel Aviv heard a violin on the radio and begged his parents for one. They were too poor, so Itzhak Perlman found a toy fiddle in a junk shop and taught himself to play. By the time he was ten, polio had ravaged his legs, leaving him dependent on crutches and braces for the rest of his life. Concert halls weren't built for someone who couldn't walk to the stage. He played anyway.

At thirteen, Perlman appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show in America — a boy from Israel on crutches, dazzling millions. But the real test came years later, during a concert at Lincoln Center. Mid-performance, one of his violin strings snapped. The audience expected him to stop, to limp offstage and replace it. Instead, Perlman closed his eyes, paused for a moment, and then signaled the conductor to begin again. He rearranged the entire piece in his head on the spot, coaxing sounds from three strings that most violinists couldn't manage with four.

When he finished, the hall erupted. A journalist later asked him why he didn't simply stop and restring. Perlman reportedly said: 'You know, sometimes it is the artist's task to find out how much music you can still make with what you have left.' That single sentence became a philosophy — not just for musicians, but for anyone who has ever been told their limitations define them.

Perlman went on to win sixteen Grammy Awards, play for presidents and queens, and teach the next generation at Juilliard. He never once pretended his disability didn't exist. He simply refused to let it be the most interesting thing about him. Every time he labored to the stage on crutches, settled into his chair, and lifted his bow, he was making the same quiet argument: the music matters more than the struggle to reach it.
